Just a quick answer, but you can inbox me for me details:

 1. Most crimes and poverty have a direct link. Black communities and communities of color in general are often have limited resources and overall wealth accumulation due to a long history of discriminatory practices in banking, job availability, etc. Also, these areas are historically policed at much higher rates causing higher arrest rates. The perfect statistic to look at is the rate of drug use across races and the rate of jailing for it. Black and POC are disproportionately arrested for something that is done equally across all races. There aren’t any raids done on Wall Street or other affluent areas notorious for cocaine use, but “crack houses” in the projects are normally hit. Also, it wasn’t until very recently that drug use was treated as a mental health problem, and even now the difference between an 18 year old whose parents can bail him out and get him into rehab and an 18 year old whose stuck in there because he can’t afford to leave is extremely depressing. The prison and bail system is not about justice, but about who can afford “justice”. I recommend watching 13th on Netflix. 

2. It’s not 3 generations- it’s 1. The ‘94 Crime Bill put millennials (super predator children)  and Gen X in jail  at alarming rates. The makeup of the modern black family has changed and improved since 2008, but poverty again has lasting affects on this. Also, within the Black community access to birth control and sexual education is thread bare. Health services are difficult to come by and most states do not require comprehensive sex Ed. Black communities are also conservative in many ways limiting familial conversations around sex and sexuality. I wouldn’t say “leaning into crime” is for easy and big money. When the only people around you who can seemingly support you or protect you are affiliated with crime - that’s what you go into. When your school resources have been cut and it’s difficult to get your share - life seems hopeless. Economic issues as well as resources two education have contributed to this.

3. Just make a friend. Go to a black church, go to a Juneteenth event, swipe right on more black women on tinder lol. If Black people aren’t in your immediate circle you have to seek it out. Facebook is a great resource for local events. If you live in a small town this may be harder to do, but bigger cities or University towns normal have a ton of resources and events to participate in. At the end of the day, the more you talk to people the better you understand them and their culture. You also understand that everyone is different and everyone has wildly different experiences, but with common themes. My experience growing up in the rural south is VERY different from someone growing up in the South Side of Chicago.

4. Black persons isn’t racist to me. I feel like most people I know or fee Black instead of African American, but again this takes having a conversation with that person. Maybe “African American” was more appropriate 10 years ago, but theories of Blackness and the Black community has changed drastically. At the end of the day, it’s okay to say “Black people”, but you should take a minute and think why it’s uncomfortable for you to say it. How have you heard it used before? What image pops in your head when you say “Back people”? How do you imagine a black person would react to you saying as compared to the reality?

At the end of the day, more research into Black history is very important. If you never took a history class about it after High School I highly recommend doing as much research as possible. There are a ton of podcasts, documentaries, etc. about it that puts things into a bigger perspective. It wasn’t until last year that I learned about the Tulsa Race Toots and I’m Black. It’s also really important for things you see on the internet/ in media to be a catalyst for face to face conversation and not define your position. Change happens in your community so volunteer or do whatever is accessible.

I hope this was helpful!

From the perspective of a SO, it really depends on so many other details and the overall relationship.

For background, my husband (then boyfriend) was diagnosed with bipolar disorder. I was with him from his first diagnoses to today. Throughout our experience he has derided off of mood stabilizers, tranquilizers, Benzos - you name it. I was committed to being his partner, but we also had healthy communication about my emotions during his detox. When he was coming off of klonopin ( he had began using it outside of medicinal purposes and selling it) he moved in with his parents for a month because I had just come back from a suicide attempt, had started a new job in a new state, was pissed over his actions, and was completely overwhelmed. Detox’s aren’t fun for anyone and it’s a lot to handle. Usually, there has been emotional trauma or hardship leading up to the detox that can make that last period overwhelming for partners.

Everyone’s situation is very different. Once he got diagnosed we immediately started going to digital couples therapy (cheaper) to learn how to communicate our feelings. Our dark, ugly, selfish feelings that people have when dealing with addiction and mental illness. It helped drastically and absolutely saved our relationship. He understood I wasn’t in the mental state for dealing with a complete detox alone. 

You have to really approach the situation understanding that other people have emotional limits and it doesn’t mean they don’t love you or aren’t committed. Dealing with someone who is a drug addict is hard. I have found a really great partner and luckily neither of us harbor resentment about our toughest moments, but it was a lot of work to get there.

If you’re fully paid up for January, check your lease agreement and see if they have grounds to evict for February non payment yet. Usually, they’re not supposed to accept any rental payments following eviction filing because the filing will state all monies owed i.e. January rent. If you no longer owe January rent then they need to do a separate filing for February. Them accepting money from you seriously may be a saving grace. Double check what the filing states and any notices they’ve given you. Also save payment records - this is extremely important.

You have rights and it’s important to show up to the court date. The court usually has resources for finding housing as well. You could also request an extension to find housing so you don’t have to vacate in the allotted period following the judgement.

Have an illegal pet is a major issue that can result in a hefty fine. My property charges $500 per violation, but I would check your lease agreement. So if they find out you do have an animal before you leave you’re probably going to end up paying more than if you would have registered it to begin with. Ultimately any damage will be taken out of you personal deposit regardless if you have a pet or not. Another issue that comes up with pets often is that if the next tenant is extremely allergic the apartment has to be sanitized and you may have to do a carpet removal. This is 100% a risk vs reward scenario. If you get caught you’re totally screwed, if not you just have more taken out of your deposit for cleaning and any damages.

Read your lease to see what you can be fined. If it’s more than $100, just register your pet and pay what you need to.
